title.narrative: Herat Eartquake Joint Response - Cordaid implementation

description.narrative:
A magnitude 6.3 earthquake, with the epicenter in Zindajan district, 40 km west from Herat city, and a series of strong aftershocks, occurred on Saturday the 7th of October 2023. The earthquake took place in the morning, when mostly women and children are at home, and men were out. Especially around the epicentre, whole villages have been whipped out, as houses are traditionally made of clay and cement, which could not resist these shocks. While search and rescue was still full ongoing, on the 11th of October another 6.3 magnitude earthquake took place, with the epicentre 28km north of Herat city. And on the 15th of October another 6.3 magnitude earthquake happened, this time in Injil district, which is adjacent to Zindajan district and was also one of the most affected district of the first earthquake.
According to the Herat Earthquake Joint Response Plan (OCHA, 10/2023), an estimated 319 villages were impacted by the earthquakes. Some villages have seen practically all houses collapsed, in others houses are still standing but are severely damaged. As per the OCHA flash update #5 & #7, so far an estimated 21,500 homes are are completely destroyed by the earthquake; 1.384 have died during the multiple earthquakes, and 1.853 people are injured. Injured people are/were treated outside the hospital because there is not enough room in the hospital and also people are scared of being inside buildings.
Infrastructure is also damaged, as power supply was cut, as well as phone networks, and other basic infrastructure seriously damaged: water supply, roads, health facilities, schools. Many people have been sleeping outside or in tents since the first earthquake, and have poor access to hygiene facilities, increasing public health as well as protection risks. There is risk for the outbreak of respiratory and waterborne diseases (Health Cluster 09/10/2023). Should displacement continue over the coming weeks, people in temporary shelters will also be facing the imminent cold season (WB accessed 09/10/2023; AP 10/10/2023). It should not be underestimated that winter is approaching, rains have started, which is having also an impact of people staying outside or living in destroyed houses, as temperatures are dropping as well. The earthquakes have come at the start of the lean season, at the beginning of the winter, which is seriously affected people’s coping mechanisms.
At the moment the multiple-partner, joint needs assessment in the affected districts, coordinated by OCHA, is still ongoing. OCHA has released the Earthquake Response Plan, while the assessments are ongoing, in which 114.000 people have been identified as affected. From DRA partner staff on the ground, it has been said that only 25% of the affected area/population has been assessed (date 19/10/2023). This also due to the damages to infrastructure (bridges also collapsed), and landslides that occurred destroying the main highway between Herat and Torghundi, and lastly, there is limited possibility for accommodation in the areas around the epicentre of the earthquake, causing assessors (and also responders) to have to return to Herat at the end of the day. DRA and local partner staff on the ground therefore jointly reached out to staff and local district officials to collect data directly from these sources to have a better estimated from the people severely affected. This resulted in an overview of people affected per district, reaching a total of 286.790 people severely affected – their houses are completely destroyed or severely damaged; the expectation is that this number will still increase (estimated population in the affected area is 1,021,896, within a 50km radius of the earthquake area).
Afghanistan as a whole face a complex humanitarian crisis, as the country needs to recover from over 40 years of war, and at the same time the impact of drought and natural disasters. The takeover of the government by the Taliban in 2021, and the economic collapse that followed, has put people in negative coping mechanisms, with more than half of the population in need of assistance. High levels of unemployment and sustained inflation of key commodities have caused the average household debt to increase, challenging people’s coping mechanisms and thwarting the already fragile economy’s ability to adapt to shocks. Protection threats are also on the rise, especially women and girls are at risk of losing their rights and protection. In Herat, according to the latest IPC report of May ’23, 40% of the population is facing high levels of acute food insecurity, which was already projected to increase during the winter months. People have little resilience remaining to cope with yet another shock.

Partners are targeting the most affected districts, where the majority of the population has been severely affected by the earthquake. Therefore, close consultation with community representatives, through amongst others beneficiary selection committees, will support with prioritizing the most vulnerable households in the targeted villages/communities.
Across activities, specific attention will be given to ensure vulnerable groups can access & receive services in a safe way & in line with the cultural context. Selection of the targeted population will prioritize marginalized groups, including women (PLW and Female HH), children, PWDs & elderly, and challenges to access aid, and them distribution process will ensure these marginalized individuals are the HH member receiving the MPC/NFI when feasible.
The total number of individuals targeted in Injil, Kushk and Zindajan districts is 55,350, without double counting. For more information, please refer to the consolidated logframe for this joint response.

The key objective of this Acute Herat Earthquakes Joint Response is to provide life-saving assistance to people severely affected by multiple earthquakes in Injil, Kushk and Zindajan districts of Herat.

title.narrative: ACC-R1: Number of crisis-affected people who are also involved in the design, implementation, monitoring and/or evaluation of the programme

description.narrative: Participation is defined as the involvement of crisis-affected people in one or more phases of the programme: assessment, design, implementation, monitoring or evaluation. Participation does not take place when activities are carried out in exchange for a salary of 'in-kind' payment unless the affected people are involved in decision-making processes and have an impact on decisions that affect them. Please describe in the activity description what this involvement specifically entails and in which phase of the program conflict-affected people are involved.

title.narrative: CSH-R1: Number of people benefitting from unconditional and unrestricted cash transfers

description.narrative: Unconditional transfers are provided to beneficiaries without the recipient having to do anything in return in order to receive the assistance . Unrestricted transfers can be used entirely as the recipient chooses i.e. there are no restrictions on how the transfer is spent (Definitions of CALP). It can be delivered e.g. through local banks, shops, traders, local money transfer companies, remittance companies and post offices in either one or several instalments.

title.narrative: WSH-R4: Number of people having access to sufficient and safe water for domestic use

description.narrative: Access: maximum distance to water point 500m, queuing time less than 15min, filling time maximum 3 min/20 litres or as locally agreed. Water access should be during the whole period of implementation unless action is mostly related to building the local water delivery capacity. Sufficient: covering basic needs, i.e. 7.5-15 l/p/d or as locally agreed. Safe: 1) low risk of faecal contamination, 2) No faecal coliforms detectable in any 100-ml sample, 3) For piped water supplies, or for all water supplies at times of risk or presence of diarrhoea epidemic, water is treated with a disinfectant to achieve free chlorine residual at the tap of 0.5 mg per litre and turbidity is below 5 NTU, 4) If for a short period, water which is contaminated chemically or radiologically is used, no (significant probability of) negative health effect is (likely to be) detected. Domestic use: drinking, cooking and personal hygiene (incl. laundry)

title.narrative: WSH-R6: Number of people reached with hygiene promotion/awareness raising activities

description.narrative: Hygiene promotion/awareness raising activities. Could be training, campaigns, radio broadcasts, flyers etc. Excludes the distribution of Hygiene/dignity kits that should be covered under WHS-I1.

title.narrative: WSH-R1: Number of people having regular access to soap to meet hygienic needs

description.narrative: Regular and timely access: 250g soap/p/m for personal hygiene, 200g soap/p/month for laundry. This includes hygiene/dignity kits. Access may be in-kind or though voucher distribution or through unconditional restricted cash to enable beneficiary to buy soap (without compromising access to other basic needs). Distributed items need to be culturally acceptable i.e. take into account local practice and expectations.

title.narrative: WSH-R2: Number of people having access to dignified, safe, clean and functional excreta disposal facilities

description.narrative: Access: ratio (user/facility) of 1 toilet for a max. 20 people, distance < 50 metres from dwellings, or as locally agreed. Clean: regular cleaning and maintenance for public facilities. Dignified: Use of toilets respect cultural preference and is arranged by household(s) and/or segregated by sex. Unsafe facilities: unstable (unlined) pits with risk of collapse, pits accessible to vectors, pits contaminating water tables and poorly sited facilities which expose women and girls to attacks, especially at night. Functional facility: fully constructed, in working order and properly maintained, of a type and in a location acceptable to intended users, with hand washing facilities and anal cleansing material.
